title: Existence and computation of derived limits
statement: Let $\mathcal D$ be a triangulated category and let $(K_n,f_n)$ be an inverse system of objects of $\mathcal D$ [def-weil-inverse-system]. 1. If $\prod_nK_n$ exists in $\mathcal D$, then a derived limit [def-weil-derived-limit] $R\varprojlim_nK_n$ exists, and any two derived limits are isomorphic, although not canonically so. 2. Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category with exact countable products and let $\mathcal D=D(\mathcal A)$. Then countable products exist in $\mathcal D$, are represented by termwise products of any representatives, and satisfy $H^p(\prod_iK_i)\cong\prod_iH^p(K_i)$. 3. In the situation of (2), assume in addition that $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives. Let $\operatorname{Tow}(\mathcal A)$ be the abelian category whose objects are inverse systems in $\mathcal A$ and whose morphisms are compatible levelwise maps [def-weil-inverse-system]. If $I_\bullet$ is a K-injective representative in $\operatorname{Tow}(\mathcal A)$ of the tower $(K_n,f_n)$, then the termwise inverse-limit complex $\varprojlim_n I_n$ represents $R\varprojlim_nK_n$.

proof.text: For (1), the definition [def-weil-derived-limit] forms the endomorphism $1-s$ of $\prod_nK_n$ and asks for a distinguished triangle $K\xrightarrow{p}\prod_nK_n\xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_nK_n\xrightarrow{\delta}K[1]$; by TR1 of [def-weil-triangulated-category] the morphism $1-s$ lies in a distinguished triangle $\prod_nK_n\xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_nK_n\to C\to\prod_nK_n[1]$, and rotating it back by TR2 (applied to $K:=C[-1]$, with the sign absorbed by the isomorphism of triangles $(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id},-\mathrm{id})$ and TR1) gives such a triangle, so a derived limit exists. Given two derived limits $(K,p,\delta)$ and $(K',p',\delta')$, rotate both Roos triangles by TR2 so that the two product terms come first; TR3 of [def-weil-triangulated-category] (equivalently [lem-weil-pbc-triangle-morphism-extension]) extends the pair $(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})$ on the product terms to a morphism of the rotated triangles, whose third component is $\varphi[1]$ for some $\varphi:K\to K'$. Two of its components are identities, so [lem-sf-triangle-morphism-iso] (Tag 014A) makes $\varphi[1]$, hence $\varphi$, an isomorphism. The extension supplied by TR3 is not unique, so the isomorphism is not canonical.

For (2), choose complexes $C_i$ representing $K_i$ and let $\prod_iC_i$ be the termwise product with projections $\mathrm{pr}_i$. Exactness of countable products makes the products of the short exact sequences $0\to Z^p\to C^p\to B^{p+1}\to0$ and $0\to B^p\to Z^p\to H^p\to0$ exact, so $Z^p$, $B^p$ and $H^p$ commute with products: $H^p(\prod_iC_i)=\prod_iH^p(C_i)$, and a product of quasi-isomorphisms is a quasi-isomorphism. A chain map into a termwise product, and a chain homotopy, are exactly families of component chain maps and homotopies, so $\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal A)}(L,\prod_iN_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal A)}(L,N_i)$. Quasi-isomorphisms form a multiplicative system in $K(\mathcal A)$ with localization $D(\mathcal A)$ [lem-pc-quasi-isomorphisms-multiplicative-system, def-weil-abstract-derived-category], so every morphism $Q(X)\to Q(Y)$ is $Q(s)^{-1}Q(f)$ for a quasi-isomorphism $s:Y\to M$ and $f:X\to M$, and $Q(s)^{-1}Q(f)=0$ if and only if $uf\simeq0$ for some quasi-isomorphism $u:M\to M'$ [lem-pc-left-localization-hom-colimit]. Existence (the argument of Tag 07KC): given $\alpha_i=Q(s_i)^{-1}Q(f_i):L\to C_i$ with $s_i:C_i\to M_i$, the product $s=\prod_is_i$ is a quasi-isomorphism and $\alpha=Q(s)^{-1}Q(\prod_if_i)$ satisfies $Q(\mathrm{pr}_i)\alpha=\alpha_i$, because $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ s=s_i\circ\mathrm{pr}_i$. Uniqueness: let $\alpha=Q(s)^{-1}Q(f):L\to\prod_iC_i$, $s:\prod_iC_i\to M$, with $Q(\mathrm{pr}_i)\alpha=0$ for all $i$. Write $Q(\mathrm{pr}_i)Q(s)^{-1}=Q(t_i)^{-1}Q(g_i)$ with $t_i:C_i\to N_i$ a quasi-isomorphism and $g_i:M\to N_i$; then $Q(g_is)=Q(t_i\mathrm{pr}_i)$ and $Q(g_if)=0$, so after composing $t_i,g_i$ with a later quasi-isomorphism out of $N_i$ we have $g_is\simeq t_i\mathrm{pr}_i$ and $g_if\simeq0$. With $g=(g_i)_i:M\to\prod_iN_i$ and the quasi-isomorphism $t=\prod_it_i$, componentwise homotopies give $gs\simeq t$ and $gf\simeq0$, so $Q(s)^{-1}=Q(t)^{-1}Q(g)$ and $\alpha=Q(t)^{-1}Q(gf)=0$. As $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal A)}$ is additive, $\prod_iC_i$ with the $Q(\mathrm{pr}_i)$ is the product of the $K_i$ in $D(\mathcal A)$ [def-weil-category-product], for any choice of representatives.

For (3), for each $n$ the functor $\lambda_n:\mathcal A\to\operatorname{Tow}(\mathcal A)$ sending $X$ to the tower equal to $X$ at levels $m\le n$ with identity transitions and $0$ at levels $m>n$ is exact and left adjoint to evaluation $\operatorname{ev}_n$ (a map $\lambda_nX\to Y_\bullet$ is determined by its level-$n$ component $X\to Y_n$), so [lem-weil-pbc-right-adjoint-preserves-kinjective] makes each $\operatorname{ev}_n(I_\bullet)$ K-injective. By [lem-pc-ringed-space-product-kinjective] (a general abelian category, applied to the countable index set of levels, whose termwise products exist by hypothesis) the termwise product $P=\prod_n\operatorname{ev}_n(I_\bullet)$ is K-injective and represents $\prod_nK_n$ in $D(\mathcal A)$ with the projections, as also given by Step 2; the chain map $1-s:P\to P$ satisfies $\mathrm{pr}_n\circ(1-s)=\mathrm{pr}_n-f_n\circ\mathrm{pr}_{n+1}$, so it represents the transition endomorphism of [def-weil-derived-limit].

The mapping cone of the chain map $1-s:P\to P$ gives the distinguished cone triangle $P\xrightarrow{1-s}P\to\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)\to P[1]$ of $D(\mathcal A)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]; rotating it back by TR2 of [def-weil-triangulated-category] gives a distinguished triangle $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)[-1]\to P\xrightarrow{1-s}P\to\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)$, so by Step 3 the object $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)[-1]$ is a derived limit of $(K_n,f_n)$ [def-weil-derived-limit]. By [lem-weil-derived-limit-roos-complex] the termwise inverse-limit complex $L=\varprojlim_nI_n$ is quasi-isomorphic to $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)[-1]$, so it represents the same object of $D(\mathcal A)$, namely $R\varprojlim_nK_n$.
